claim: LIMK1 contains a conserved palmitoyl-motif at adjacent cysteine residues Cys7 and Cys8.
source: LIMK1 was a prominent hit in both searches and adjacent cysteine residues (Cys7, Cys8, conserved in all vertebrate LIMK1 orthologs) were predicted to be palmitoylated (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic predictions and sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LIMK1 is palmitoylated at Cys7/Cys8.
source: Wt-LIMK1-myc was clearly detected in ABE fractions, indicative of palmitoylation, but was not detected in control purifications in which the essential ABE reagent hydroxylamine (NH2OH) was omitted (Figure 1B). In contrast, CCSS-LIMK1-myc was not detected in ABE fractions (Figure 1B), suggesting that LIMK1 is palmitoylated at Cys7/Cys8.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABE assay data showing that wild-type LIMK1 is detected in ABE fractions while the CCSS mutant is not.

claim: LIMK1 palmitoylation coincides with spine development and maturation in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, despite similar LIMK1 protein expression across these developmental stages, palmitoyl-LIMK1 was not detected in ABE fractions from DIV4 neurons (Figure 1C). However, palmitoyl-LIMK1 became detectable at DIV8, increased markedly at DIV12 and remained prominent at DIV20 (Figure 1C). These findings suggest that LIMK1 is palmitoylated in hippocampal neurons and that its palmitoylation coincides with spine development and maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABE assay data across different developmental stages (DIV4, DIV8, DIV12, DIV20) showing temporal correlation with spine formation.

claim: LIMK1 is robustly palmitoylated in adult rat forebrain.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the robust palmitoylation of LIMK1 in adult rat forebrain homogenates (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABE assay data from adult rat forebrain tissue.

claim: Palmitoylation targets LIMK1 to dendritic spines.
source: In support of this hypothesis, wt-LIMK1 was highly enriched in spines but CCSS-LIMK1 was not (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing differential spine localization of wild-type versus CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: Palmitoylation anchors LIMK1 in spines to limit its diffusion.
source: We reasoned that palmitoylation might anchor LIMK1 in spines to limit its diffusion, thus enhancing spatial control of actin regulation. We therefore transfected neurons with GFP-tagged LIMK1 and monitored its diffusibility by Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) using time-lapse imaging. Prominent FRAP, indicative of diffusion of the tagged protein, was observed with CCSS-LIMK1-GFP but not with wt-LIMK1-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experiments showing reduced mobility of wild-type LIMK1 compared to CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: CCSS mutation decreases the stable fraction of LIMK1-GFP in spines.
source: Quantitative analysis of FRAP data confirmed that CCSS mutation decreased the stable fraction of LIMK1-GFP in spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative FRAP analysis.

claim: Protein-protein interactions are important to constrain LIMK1 in spines.
source: We note that the time course of LIMK1-GFP FRAP, irrespective of its palmitoylation status, is markedly slower than previously characterized soluble proteins (Star et al., 2002; Bingol et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2010). This suggests that other factors, most likely protein–protein interactions, are important to constrain LIMK1 in spines.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of FRAP kinetics with previously published data for soluble proteins.

claim: 2-Bromopalmitate reduces LIMK1 palmitoylation in neurons.
source: The palmitoylation inhibitor 2-Bromopalmitate (2-Br; [Jennings et al., 2009]) did not affect endogenous LIMK1 protein levels, but greatly reduced LIMK1 palmitoylation in neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), reinforcing the conclusion that LIMK1 is palmitoylated.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABE assay data following 2-Br treatment.

claim: 2-Bromopalmitate greatly reduces wild-type LIMK1 spine targeting without affecting overall spine numbers.
source: In parallel experiments, 2-Br greatly reduced wt-LIMK1 spine targeting without affecting overall spine numbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and spine density quantification following 2-Br treatment.

claim: Cys7/Cys8 palmitoylation is required for LIMK1 spine targeting.
source: The similar effects of CCSS mutation and 2-Br treatment strongly suggest that Cys7/Cys8 palmitoylation is required for LIMK1 spine targeting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similar effects of genetic mutation and pharmacological inhibition.

claim: LIMK1 deletion mutants lacking the kinase domain (LIMK1-1-258) or lacking the kinase and PDZ domains (LIMK1 1-137) localize to spines as effectively as full-length LIMK1.
source: LIMK1-GFP deletion mutants lacking the kinase domain (LIMK1-1-258) or lacking the kinase and PDZ domains (LIMK1 1-137) localized to spines as effectively as full-length LIMK1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing spine localization of deletion mutants.

claim: LIMK1's N-terminal 15 amino acid sequence is sufficient to target GFP to spines.
source: Remarkably, a minimal palmitoylation motif construct lacking the kinase, PDZ and LIM domains (LIMK1 [1–15]-GFP; Figure 2A–C) was sufficient to target GFP to spines. In contrast, cytosolic GFP was not enriched in spines (Figure 2A–C). These findings indicate that LIMK1's N-terminal 15 amino acid sequence is a specific spine targeting motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing that the minimal 1-15 construct targets GFP to spines.

claim: C7S- and C8S-LIMK1 mutants are not targeted to spines.
source: Consistent with this notion, C7S- and C8S-LIMK1 mutants were not targeted to spines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing lack of spine enrichment for single cysteine mutants.

claim: Myr-CCSS-LIMK1 is not targeted to spines.
source: Moreover, a CCSS-LIMK1 mutant carrying a sequence that directs addition of the lipid myristate (Myr-CCSS-LIMK1), which can mimic a single palmitoylation event (Thomas et al., 2012), was not targeted to spines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing lack of spine enrichment for Myr-CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: Myr-SC-LIMK1 and Myr-CS-LIMK1 mutants are not enriched in spines.
source: Lastly, we examined the spine targeting of N-terminal mutants of LIMK1 that are predicted to be doubly lipid-modified with myristate plus single palmitate (Myr-SC-LIMK1, Myr-CS-LIMK1). Neither of these mutants was enriched in spines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing lack of spine enrichment for doubly lipid-modified mutants.

claim: An intact CC palmitoyl-motif is critical for spine LIMK1 targeting.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that an intact CC palmitoyl-motif is critical for spine LIMK1 targeting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple mutant analyses showing that only dual palmitoylation at the CC motif enables spine targeting.

claim: LIMK1 is detected in rat brain Post-Synaptic Density (PSD) fractions.
source: Consistent with this notion, LIMK1 was detected in rat brain Post-Synaptic Density (PSD) fractions, including the PSDIII fraction, which is enriched in spine-associated proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data showing LIMK1 in PSD fractions.

claim: LIMK2 is absent from PSD fractions.
source: In contrast, LIMK2 was absent from PSD fractions (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and was not enriched in spines (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation and immunocytochemistry data showing LIMK2 is not in PSD fractions or enriched in spines.

claim: A chimeric protein consisting of LIMK1's minimal spine targeting sequence fused to LIMK2 is readily detected in spines.
source: Strikingly, however, a chimeric protein consisting of LIMK1's minimal spine targeting sequence fused to LIMK2 was readily detected in spines (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing spine localization of the chimeric LIMK2 construct.

claim: LIMK1's palmitoyl-motif accounts for differential localization of LIMK1 and LIMK2.
source: This result suggests that LIMK1's palmitoyl-motif accounts for differential localization of the two LIMKs, potentially explaining why loss of LIMK1 causes spine-specific phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the chimera experiment showing that LIMK1's N-terminal motif is sufficient to target LIMK2 to spines.

claim: LIMK1 shRNA potently reduces levels of cotransfected rat LIMK1-myc.
source: We first identified an shRNA that potently reduced levels of cotransfected rat LIMK1-myc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced LIMK1 expression with shRNA.

claim: LIMK1 shRNA greatly reduces endogenous LIMK1 levels when packaged into lentiviral particles and used to infect hippocampal neurons.
source: The same shRNA greatly reduced endogenous LIMK1 levels when packaged into lentiviral particles and used to infect hippocampal neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced endogenous LIMK1 in infected neurons.

claim: shRNA-resistant (shr) 'rescue' forms of wt-LIMK1 and CCSS-LIMK1 are insensitive to LIMK1 shRNA.
source: shRNA-resistant (shr) 'rescue' forms of wt-LIMK1 (shr-wt-LIMK1-myc) and CCSS-LIMK1 (shr-CCSS-LIMK1-myc) were insensitive to LIMK1 shRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing that shr constructs are not knocked down by shRNA.

claim: LIMK1 knockdown significantly attenuates the recovery of GFP-actin fluorescence after photobleaching.
source: However, the recovery of GFP-actin fluorescence in LIMK1 knockdown neurons was significantly attenuated, compared to control neurons. This attenuated recovery was evident in plots of the averaged data (Figure 4D), or plots of all individual FRAP measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and is consistent with an increase in the percentage of stable GFP-actin.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data showing reduced fluorescence recovery in LIMK1 knockdown neurons.

claim: The fraction of stable actin is significantly increased in LIMK1 knockdown spines.
source: Two analytical methods confirmed that the fraction of stable actin is indeed significantly increased in LIMK1 knockdown spines (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), see also [Koskinen et al., 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative FRAP analysis using two different methods.

claim: The increase of stable GFP-actin caused by LIMK1 knockdown is restored to control levels by shr-wt-LIMK1, but not by shr-CCSS-LIMK1.
source: Strikingly, the increase of stable GFP-actin caused by LIMK1 knockdown was restored to control levels by shr-wt-LIMK1, but not by shr-CCSS-LIMK1 (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data showing rescue by wild-type but not CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: The half-time of GFP-actin fluorescence recovery is not significantly different under any condition examined.
source: In contrast to these marked effects on the pool of stable actin, the half-time of GFP-actin fluorescence recovery was not significantly different under any condition examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative FRAP analysis of recovery kinetics.

claim: The predominant effect of loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 on GFP-actin turnover is to reduce the pool of mobile actin in spines.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the predominant effect of loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 on GFP-actin turnover is to reduce the pool of mobile actin in spines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from FRAP data showing increased stable fraction without change in recovery kinetics.

claim: Palmitoyl-LIMK1 is essential for normal actin turnover in spines.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that palmitoyl-LIMK1 is essential for normal actin turnover in spines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from FRAP experiments showing impaired actin dynamics in the absence of palmitoyl-LIMK1.

claim: Focal uncaging of MNI-glutamate on spines induces a rapid, lasting volume increase of the stimulated spine in control neurons.
source: In biolistically transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing the morphology marker mCherry, focal uncaging of MNI-glutamate on spines induced a rapid, lasting volume increase of the stimulated spine, similar to published results (135 ± 7% of initial volume, 15–25 min post-uncaging; Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon imaging data showing spine volume changes following glutamate uncaging.

claim: An uncaging protocol pairing to 0 mV in whole-cell recordings leads to a persistent increase in the volume of the stimulated spine accompanied by a spine-specific increase in the amplitude of uncaging-evoked postsynaptic currents.
source: An analogous uncaging protocol (i.e., pairing to 0 mV in whole-cell recordings) likewise led to a persistent increase in the volume of the stimulated spine that was accompanied by a spine-specific increase in the amplitude of uncaging-evoked postsynaptic currents (uEPSCs; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology and imaging data showing coordinated structural and functional plasticity.

claim: Activity-dependent spine enlargement is significantly attenuated in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing LIMK1 shRNA.
source: In CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing mCherry plus LIMK1 shRNA, activity-dependent spine enlargement was significantly attenuated (116 ± 6% of initial volume, 15–25 min post-uncaging; p = 0.032 vs control neurons, Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon imaging data showing reduced spine enlargement in LIMK1 knockdown neurons.

claim: LIMK1 is required for activity-dependent spine enlargement.
source: This result suggests that LIMK1 is required for activity-dependent spine enlargement, consistent with the importance of actin polymerization in this process (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the knockdown experiment and is consistent with prior literature on actin polymerization.

claim: Activity-dependent spine enlargement can be rescued by shr-wt-LIMK1 but not by shr-CCSS-LIMK1.
source: Strikingly, activity-dependent spine enlargement could be rescued by shr-wt-LIMK1 (control: 136 ± 6%; wt-LIMK1 rescue: 140 ± 8%, p = 0.496, Mann–Whitney U test) but not by shr-CCSS-LIMK1 (interleaved control: 141 ± 10%; CCSS-LIMK1: 115 ± 4%, p = 0.031, Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 5C–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon imaging data showing rescue by wild-type but not CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: Palmitoyl-LIMK1 is required for activity-dependent spine enlargement.
source: These findings suggest that palmitoyl-LIMK1 is required for activity-dependent spine enlargement.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from rescue experiments showing that only palmitoylatable LIMK1 can restore activity-dependent spine enlargement.

claim: Acute loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 does not affect dendritic spine number.
source: Acute loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 markedly impaired spine actin turnover without affecting dendritic spine number (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density quantification 24 hours after transfection.

claim: Prolonged LIMK1 knockdown significantly reduces dendritic spine density.
source: To address this possibility, we transfected mature neurons to express GFP plus/minus LIMK1 shRNA and examined spine density 5 days later. This prolonged LIMK1 knockdown significantly reduced dendritic spine density, which was rescued by cotransfected shr-wt-LIMK1 but not by shr-CCSS-LIMK1 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by spine density quantification 5 days after transfection.

claim: Absence of LIMK1 concomitantly reduces the number of excitatory synapses.
source: Absence of LIMK1 concomitantly reduced the number of excitatory synapses (defined as spines positive for pre- and postsynaptic markers; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalized PSD-95 and synapsin I puncta.

claim: Loss of both spines and synapses is rescued by shr-wt-LIMK1 but not shr-CCSS-LIMK1.
source: Loss of both spines and synapses was rescued by shr-wt-LIMK1 but not shr-CCSS-LIMK1 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of spine density and synaptic puncta in rescue experiments.

claim: Prolonged loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 leads to spine instability and synapse loss.
source: Together, these results suggest that prolonged loss of palmitoyl-LIMK1 leads to spine instability and synapse loss.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from long-term knockdown experiments showing reduced spine and synapse numbers.

claim: PAK3 phosphorylates wt-LIMK1 and CCSS-LIMK1 with similar kinetics and to a similar extent in vitro.
source: In in vitro kinase assays, LIMK1's upstream activator PAK3 phosphorylated wt-LIMK1 and CCSS-LIMK1 with similar kinetics and to a similar extent (assessed by a phospho-specific antibody recognizing LIMK1's activation site (T508); Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing similar phosphorylation of wild-type and CCSS-LIMK1 by PAK3.

claim: Following activation by PAK3, wt- and CCSS-LIMK1 phosphorylate cofilin to a similar extent in vitro.
source: Moreover, following activation by PAK3, wt- and CCSS-LIMK1 phosphorylated their downstream substrate cofilin to a similar extent in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing similar cofilin phosphorylation by wild-type and CCSS-LIMK1.

claim: CCSS mutation does not affect LIMK1's phosphorylation by PAK3 or LIMK1's ability to phosphorylate cofilin in vitro.
source: These results suggest that CCSS mutation affects neither LIMK1's phosphorylation by PAK3, nor LIMK1's ability to phosphorylate cofilin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: CCSS mutation is unlikely to grossly affect LIMK1 structure.
source: It is thus also unlikely that CCSS mutation grossly affects LIMK1 structure.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that CCSS-LIMK1 retains enzymatic activity in vitro.

claim: T508 phosphorylation of wt-LIMK1 in hippocampal neurons is approximately 10-fold higher than that of CCSS-LIMK1.
source: In striking contrast, T508 phosphorylation of wt-LIMK1 in hippocampal neurons was approximately 10-fold higher than that of CCSS-LIMK1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data from transfected neurons.

claim: SC-LIMK1, CS-LIMK1 and Myr-CCSS-LIMK1 mutants are only weakly phosphorylated in neurons.
source: SC-LIMK1, CS-LIMK1 and Myr-CCSS-LIMK1 mutants were also only weakly phosphorylated in neurons (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data from transfected neurons.

claim: Doubly lipid-modified mutants (Myr-CS-LIMK1) are phosphorylated to a slightly greater extent than CCSS-LIMK1, but still significantly less than wild type LIMK1.
source: The doubly lipid-modified mutants, in particular Myr-CS-LIMK1, were phosphorylated to a slightly greater extent than CCSS-LIMK1, but still significantly less than wild type LIMK1 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data from transfected neurons.

claim: Spine targeting (which is only achieved by dual palmitoylation), and not membrane association per se, is the key factor that controls LIMK1 phosphorylation and activation in neurons.
source: These results suggest that spine targeting (which is only achieved by dual palmitoylation), and not membrane association per se, is the key factor that controls LIMK1 phosphorylation and activation in neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that only dually palmitoylated LIMK1 is efficiently phosphorylated in neurons.

claim: PAK inhibition greatly reduces LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, PAK inhibition, but not ROCK inhibition, greatly reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that PAK is the key LIMK1 activator in spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments showing reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation with PAK inhibitor.

claim: ROCK inhibition does not reduce LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, PAK inhibition, but not ROCK inhibition, greatly reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that PAK is the key LIMK1 activator in spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments showing no effect of ROCK inhibitor on LIMK1 phosphorylation.

claim: PAK is the key LIMK1 activator in spines.
source: Interestingly, PAK inhibition, but not ROCK inhibition, greatly reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that PAK is the key LIMK1 activator in spines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from pharmacological inhibition experiments and is supported by prior literature.

claim: CaMKII inhibition greatly reduces LIMK1 phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons.
source: Moreover, consistent with findings that spine morphological plasticity requires CaMKII (Lee et al., 2009), a CaMKII inhibitor also greatly reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments showing reduced LIMK1 phosphorylation with CaMKII inhibitor.

claim: CaMKII in spines triggers Rac/Cdc42 activation, which recruits active PAK to phosphorylate and activate wtLIMK1 specifically on the spine membrane.
source: Together, these findings suggest that CaMKII in spines triggers Rac/Cdc42 activation, which recruits active PAK to phosphorylate and activate wtLIMK1 specifically on the spine membrane.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from pharmacological inhibition experiments and integration with prior knowledge of signaling pathways.

claim: Palmitoylation controls not only LIMK1 localization but also its activation by PAK in neurons.
source: Strikingly, palmitoylation controls not only LIMK1 localization but also its activation by PAK in neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing that palmitoylation is required for both spine targeting and efficient phosphorylation of LIMK1.

claim: Palmitoylation of LIMK1 ensures spatially precise actin regulation at the single spine and potentially also the subspine levels.
source: This novel 'dual-control' mechanism ensures spatially precise actin regulation at the single spine and potentially also the subspine levels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined effects of palmitoylation on LIMK1 localization and activation.

claim: Changes in the size and shape of individual spines are closely associated with Long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: Changes in the size and shape of individual spines are closely associated with Long-term potentiation (LTP), a cellular correlate of learning and memory (Fifková and Van Harreveld, 1977; Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001; Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Bosch and Hayashi, 2012; Murakoshi and Yasuda, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Abnormal spine morphology and/or density are hallmarks of Intellectual Disability and other cognitive dysfunctions, including Autism-Spectrum Disorders and schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, abnormal spine morphology and/or density are hallmarks of Intellectual Disability and other cognitive dysfunctions, including Autism-Spectrum Disorders and schizophrenia (Fiala et al., 2002; Penzes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Precise regulation of dendritic spine morphology and number is critical for normal cognition.
source: These findings suggest that precise regulation of dendritic spine morphology and number is critical for normal cognition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the association between spine abnormalities and cognitive dysfunction.

claim: Dynamic modulation of the actin cytoskeleton is crucial for controlling spine formation and elimination, as well as modifications of the size, shape and motility of existing spines.
source: Spines are highly enriched in actin filaments, and dynamic modulation of the actin cytoskeleton is crucial for controlling not only spine formation and elimination, but also modifications of the size, shape and motility of existing spines (Hotulainen and Hoogenraad, 2010; Bosch and Hayashi, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons can rapidly alter the morphology of individual spines in response to local synaptic cues.
source: In response to local synaptic cues, neurons can rapidly alter the morphology of individual spines (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Honkura et al., 2008; Murakoshi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spine-specific regulation of actin dynamics likely requires precise spatial regulation of proteins that increase actin polymerization and those that sever/disassemble actin filaments in a given spine.
source: This process likely requires precise spatial regulation of proteins that increase actin polymerization and those that sever/disassemble actin filaments in a given spine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that neurons can rapidly alter individual spine morphology.

claim: Many actin regulators are predicted to be soluble, diffusible proteins, which appear poorly suited to operate with the necessary spatial specificity.
source: However, many actin regulators are predicted to be soluble, diffusible proteins, which appear poorly suited to operate with the necessary spatial specificity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from protein structure predictions and the requirement for spatial specificity.

claim: Palmitoylation is a protein-lipid modification that targets cytosolic proteins to specific membranes.
source: One mechanism to control protein localization is palmitoylation, a protein-lipid modification that targets cytosolic proteins to specific membranes (Fukata and Fukata, 2010; Thomas and Huganir, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Palmitoylation appears to be especially important in neurons because human genetic mutations and mouse knockouts of Palmitoyl acyltransferases (PATs) frequently lead to neurological and/or cognitive deficits.
source: Palmitoylation occurs in all eukaryotic cells but appears to be especially important in neurons because human genetic mutations and mouse knockouts of Palmitoyl acyltransferases (PATs, which catalyze palmitoylation) frequently lead to neurological and/or cognitive deficits (Fukata and Fukata, 2010; Greaves and Chamberlain, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LIMK1 and LIMK2 phosphorylate and inactivate the actin severing protein cofilin, thus promoting actin polymerization.
source: Two important actin regulatory proteins are the LIM kinases (LIMK1 and LIMK2 [Tada and Sheng, 2006]), which phosphorylate and inactivate the actin severing protein cofilin, thus promoting actin polymerization (Mizuno et al., 1994; Arber et al., 1998; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LIMK1 knockout in mice or genetic mutation in humans is associated with spine abnormalities and cognitive impairments.
source: Interestingly, LIMK1 appears particularly important for actin regulation in spines, because LIMK1 knockout in mice or genetic mutation in humans is associated with spine abnormalities and cognitive impairments (Frangiskakis et al., 1996; Tassabehji et al., 1996; Meng et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spine abnormalities and intellectual impairments are linked to mutations in PAK3.
source: Moreover, although LIMK1's upstream activator in neurons is unclear, spine abnormalities and intellectual impairments are also linked to mutations in PAK3 (Allen et al., 1998; Boda et al., 2004), a member of the p21-activated kinase (PAK) family that phosphorylates and activates LIMK1 in non-neuronal cells (Edwards et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PAK3 phosphorylates and activates LIMK1 in non-neuronal cells.
source: Moreover, although LIMK1's upstream activator in neurons is unclear, spine abnormalities and intellectual impairments are also linked to mutations in PAK3 (Allen et al., 1998; Boda et al., 2004), a member of the p21-activated kinase (PAK) family that phosphorylates and activates LIMK1 in non-neuronal cells (Edwards et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PAKs and LIMKs are predicted soluble, cytosolic proteins.
source: However, PAKs and LIMKs are predicted soluble, cytosolic proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from protein structure predictions.

claim: LIMK1 knockdown not only reduced the magnitude of activity-dependent spine enlargement, but also decreased spine growth success compared with control neurons.
source: LIMK1 knockdown not only reduced the magnitude of activity-dependent spine enlargement (Figure 6A), but also decreased spine growth success (12/26 spines; 46%) compared with control neurons (18/24 spines; 75%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual spine responses to glutamate uncaging.

claim: LIMK1 knockdown more frequently caused spine shrinkage compared with control neurons.
source: LIMK1 knockdown also more frequently caused spine shrinkage (5/26 spines; 19%) compared with control neurons (1/24 spines; 4%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual spine responses to glutamate uncaging.

claim: Spine growth success was similar in wt-LIMK1 rescue neurons and controls.
source: Spine growth success was similar in wt-LIMK1 rescue neurons (19/27 spines; 70%) and controls (15/21 spines; 71%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual spine responses to glutamate uncaging in rescue experiments.

claim: CCSS-LIMK1 'rescue' more frequently caused spine shrinkage compared with controls.
source: CCSS-LIMK1 'rescue' more frequently caused spine shrinkage (5/28 spines; 18%) compared with controls (1/23 spines; 4%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual spine responses to glutamate uncaging in rescue experiments.

claim: Repetitive focal uncaging of MNI-glutamate when neurons are clamped at 0 mV results in structural enlargement of stimulated spine but not unstimulated control spines.
source: Repetitive focal uncaging of MNI-glutamate (4 ms pulses at 720 nm, 30 pulses, 0.5 Hz) when neurons are clamped at 0 mV results in structural enlargement of stimulated spine but not unstimulated control spines (spine volume at 10–20 min post LTP; stimulated spines: 141.3 ± 7.4% of baseline, n = 11 spines, p < 0.01; unstimulated spines: 106.4 ± 9.6% of baseline, n = 11 spines, p = 0.519 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon imaging data from whole-cell recording experiments.

claim: Amplitude of uncaging-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (uEPSCs) from stimulated spines is significantly increased following single spine repetitive uncaging at 0 mV.
source: Amplitude of uncaging-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (uEPSCs) from stimulated spines (at −70 mV) was also significantly increased following single spine repetitive uncaging at 0 mV (normalized uEPSC amplitude at 10–20 min post LTP; stimulated spines: 1.31 ± 0.13, n = 11 spines, p < 0.05; unstimulated spines: 0.89 ± 5.5, n = 11 spines, p = 0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from whole-cell recording experiments.

claim: Rat LIMK1 and LIMK2 kinase domains are 70% identical and 84% similar.
source: Rat LIMK1 and LIMK2 kinase domains are 70% identical, 84% similar (NCBI BLAST).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison using NCBI BLAST.
